world_status: statement found in a copy we already had

earlier_scan.source_named: Glottolog: only Collins comparative wordlist data (1977-2003) showing Piru is a dialect of Luhu; no phonological description found.

new_statements.quote: [p.82] An important phonological rule distinguishes all Hoamoal languages from Asilulu. Stress in Hoamoal languages is always penultimate; if a suffix or particle is added to the word the stress shifts accordingly. In Asilulu this is not the case. The stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the root word; additions of suffixes do not affect this stress. For example, [moon / kind of fruit / tomorrow] Asilulu húlan e, ʔúlul e, ráwa e; Luhu huláne, ulúle, rawáʔe. Note too Asilulu palaʔekni [paláʔekən] 'recall him' and Luhu palaʔeʔena [palaʔeʔéna]. ... This obligatory penultimate stress rule ... seems to be the motivating force for certain vowel deletions in the antepenultimate syllable. [p.79] If one compares Luhu and Piru, one notices no significant sound differences.
new_statements.citation: Collins, James T. 1983. The historical relationships of the languages of Central Maluku, Indonesia. Pacific Linguistics D-47. Canberra: Australian National University.
new_statements.locator: Ch. V sec. 4 'Luhu and Hoamoal', p.82 (p.92); identity statement p.79 (p.89); cf. pp.82-83 and fn.116-117 (p.145)

At printed p.82 (p.92) the page scan reads exactly: 'An important phonological rule distinguishes all Hoamoal languages from Asilulu. For example, [moon / kind of fruit / tomorrow] Asilulu(116) húlan e, ʔúlul e, ráwa e; Luhu huláne, ulúle, rawáʔe. Note too Asilulu pal…
new_statements.rule_in_words: In Luhu (of which Piru is a dialect) and the other Hoamoal languages, stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the whole word, counting suffixes and enclitic particles/petrified postposed demonstratives (e.g. hulán-e 'moon', palaʔeʔé-na), so stress moves rightward whenever material is added; this contrasts with Asilulu, where stress stays on the root penult.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated for Luhu; Collins notes the rule interacts with the many obligatory suffixes/postparticles in Hoamoal languages (fn.117: Luhu -e is permanently suffixed to nouns ending in non-high vowels or n/t) and that it drives antepenultimate vowel deletion in a few items (kallana 'wave', sumbeke 'shove', mandae 'male').
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress including suffixes and cliticised particles (stress domain = phonological word with enclitics); based on Collins's own 1977-79 fieldnotes on Luhu and Piru; examples are citation forms. Statement is made for the Hoamoal subgroup as a whole and exemplified with Luhu; Piru is covered via Collins's explicit claim (p.79) that Piru and Luhu show no significant sound differences.
new_statements.identity_note: piru1241 'Piru' is a Glottolog bookkeeping languoid: ISO 639-3 [ppr] was merged with [lcq] Luhu (CR 2011-084, 2012-096; final name Luhu, code lcq), and Glottolog's language-level entry is luhu1243 'Luhu-Piru'. Collins 1983 (pp.79-81), from his own 1977-79 fieldwork, treats Piru (a handful of speakers over sixty at Piru village, head of Piru Bay) as a dialect of Luhu with 'no significant sound differences', differing mainly in loss of verbal conjugations and Eti/Alune loanwords. The quoted stress rule is stated for the Hoamoal branch of West Piru Bay (Luhu, Manipa, Boano, Kelang, Wakasihu) and exemplified with Luhu forms; no Piru form is cited with stress marked. Any catalog entry should be filed under luhu1243 (Luhu, Hoamoal peninsula, west Seram) with Piru as a covered dialect, not as an independent language.

new_statements.citation: Collins, James T. 2003. Language death in Maluku: The impact of the VOC. Bijdragen tot de Taal-, Land- en Volkenkunde 159(2/3): 247-289.
new_statements.check: reported on verification, not yet confirmed
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Only one work is listed (Collins 2003), and it was opened and read by the compiler; there are no other silent or unopened works to spot-check. A full-text search of the whole article for stress, accent, prominence, penult, prosody, tone and syllable found nothing beyond the p.277 notation remark and fn.11 (p.254, about Kelang/Manipa syllable reduction). Nothing missed.

new_statements.quote: [p.96] In Luhu, however, a language indigenous to the peninsula maintains a strong position. [...] The language has further innovated by permanently affixing a demonstrative, -ne ('this'), to the independent pronominal series; furthermore, articles, -e and -a, are suffixed to many nouns, with no productive alternation. This fossilization of some morphological processes has resulted in new stress patterns as well. This permanent shift in stress is probably related to the sporadic occurrence of vowel deletion in the [p.97] antepenultimate syllable which has created consonant clusters and geminate consonants; for example, **kalúlan-a > kalulána > kallána 'wave'. [p.97] [...] it can be demonstrated that Piru is a dialect of Luhu, a fact which Van Hoevell correctly stated in 1877.
new_statements.citation: Collins, James T. 1982. Linguistic Research in Maluku: A Report of Recent Field Work. Oceanic Linguistics 21(1/2): 73-146, esp. pp. 122-123 (Teor-Kur).
new_statements.locator: sec. 3.1.7 'Hoamoal', printed pp.96-97 (pp.24-25); Piru identity sentence p.97; fn.12 p.137 (no stress content)

This permanent shift in stress is probably related to the sporadic occurrence of vowel deletion in the' / p.97 'antepenultimate syllable which has created consonant clusters a…
new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the existing Collins 1983 statement (Hoamoal/Luhu stress always penultimate, shifting when a suffix or particle is added): the 1982 example kalulána / kallána places stress on the penult of the suffixed word. It adds the diachronic detail that the penult stress on fossilized-suffix forms is a 'permanent shift' which caused antepenultimate vowel deletion and consonant clusters/geminates (kallána). It also independently supports the Piru = dialect of Luhu identity on which the catalog statement relies. The remark is about Luhu, not Piru specifically; the pp.122-123 pointer in the citation concerns Teor-Kur (another listing) and has no stress content.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No explicit stress rule is stated for Piru or Luhu. The only stress remark (about Luhu, of which the paper says Piru is a dialect) is that the fossilization of suffixed articles -e/-a and demonstrative -ne produced 'new stress patterns', a 'permanent shift in stress' that then triggered sporadic antepenultimate vowel deletion; the accented example **kalúlan-a > kalulána > kallána shows stress on the penultimate syllable of the suffixed word at every stage. Reading fixed: penultimate syllable on the whole word including fossilized suffixes is inferred from the example and the shift statement, not from a stated rule.
new_statements.exceptions: none stated; the paper notes the vowel deletion is 'sporadic' and that Piru has undergone 'a number of irregular changes' and loans via Eti (Kaibobo), but says nothing about Piru stress
new_statements.identity_note: Collins 1982 p.97: 'it can be demonstrated that Piru is a dialect of Luhu, a fact which Van Hoevell correctly stated in 1877'; Piru village at the head of Piru Bay, only 'a very small number of the elderly' still remembered the language; the stress remark itself is about the Luhu language of Luhu village (>5000 residents) on the Hoamoal peninsula. Piru differs from Luhu by loss of almost all productive verbal conjugations and by East Piru Bay / Alune influence and Eti (Kaibobo) loans.
